title: The question Shvetaketu couldn't answer
hookLine: a son comes home after twelve years of study, proud and stiff, and his father asks him one question he can't answer
carry: the one thing worth knowing is brahman
tomorrow: the clay, the gold, the iron
last: PANCAGNI — ALL OF LIFE IS AN OFFERING.

cards: The front door opens. A young man comes home after twelve years away. He's twenty-four.
He has memorized the Vedas. He walks in, the text says, swollen with pride, thinking himself very learned, a little stiff with it. Maybe you've met him.
Maybe you've been him, home from the first year of college, correcting everyone at dinner. His father watches him for a while. Then he asks one question, and it isn't a test of memory.
So begins the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the most studied in Hindu philosophy: a father, a son, and two weeks of lessons.

teach.b: The father is Uddalaka Aruni, one of the great teachers of the Upanishads. The son is Shvetaketu, the same young man the king embarrassed yesterday.
When Shvetaketu was twelve, his father sent him off to study with a warning: in our family, nobody is a brahmin just by birth. Go and learn. Now he's back, proud of all he knows.
And his father asks: since you think so much of yourself, did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known?
Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. How could there be such a teaching, sir? The question isn't asking for one more fact; twelve years of facts are already in his head.
It asks whether there's one thing that, once known, makes everything else make sense.
A key, not another room. The Upanishads call what that key opens Brahman, or simply That: the one reality under everything.
And here's a teaching Hindus still live by: you can memorize scripture and still not know Brahman. Learning is facts. Knowing is something else.
And the father is gentle. He doesn't mock.
He uses a word he'll repeat through all the lessons ahead: somya, my dear, the way you'd talk to someone you love.

teach.h: THE ONE THING WORTH KNOWING IS BRAHMAN.
teach.b: Then he begins to teach with things from the kitchen and the garden. Nine times, he'll close a lesson with the same three words.

how: The sixth chapter of the Chandogya is one of the most studied texts in Hindu philosophy; Vedanta teachers often walk students through Uddalaka's lessons one at a time.

o: a title for a scholar who knows the Vedas
gentle, dear: how Uddalaka speaks to his son
a strict teacher's word for a lazy student

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the proud son, home at twenty-four
the teaching he never asked for

s: Shvetaketu came home humble and unsure
the text says he came home proud, thinking himself learned.
his father warned that nobody in the family is a brahmin just by birth
that's why he sent him away to study at twelve.
the father's question asks for one more fact
it asks for the teaching by which everything unknown becomes known.

games.q: you're Uddalaka. your son is home after twelve years, proud of everything he's memorized. what do you do?
o: praise him and throw a feast.
ask him whether he learned the teaching by which the unknown becomes known.
quiz him on the Vedas until he gets one wrong.
games.why: one question, asked gently. Shvetaketu has no answer, and the most well-known lessons of the Chandogya begin.

practice: Let what you know come up, your job, your skills, your opinions, what you studied, and set each one down beside you like books on a table; you can pick them all up later.
For now, sit with empty hands, and let the father's question hang in the air, unanswered.

wordCard.voice: Somya, gentle, dear. Uddalaka's word for his son, repeated through the lessons, as he asks whether anyone taught him the one teaching by which the unknown becomes known.

orig.note: Sanskrit somya: gentle, dear. Uddalaka's word for his son, repeated through the lessons.

carryVoice: Your line: the one thing worth knowing is Brahman. Tomorrow, his first lesson: a lump of clay. Day three hundred thirty-nine, done.
